description: An erect, grey-downy shrub about 0.5-1.5 m tall with ovate leaves, small greenish-yellow bell-shaped flowers and round orange-red berries enclosed in a papery calyx. The tuberous taproot has a horse-like smell when fresh.
cultural_significance: The Sanskrit name means 'smell of the horse', referring to the root's odour and the strength it is traditionally said to give. It is one of the best-known Rasayana (rejuvenative) herbs of Ayurveda and is often called Indian ginseng.
habitat: Dry, sandy or well-drained soils in semi-arid regions; grown as a rain-fed crop in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.

uses.title: Stress and sleep
uses.detail: Root powder with milk is traditionally used as a calming tonic for nervous exhaustion and poor sleep.

uses.title: Strength and rejuvenation
uses.detail: Described as Balya (strength-promoting) and Rasayana, given to the weak, the elderly and in convalescence.

uses.title: Joint and muscle complaints
uses.detail: Used internally and as a paste or oil externally for joint stiffness and Vata-type pain.

uses.title: Reproductive health tonic
uses.detail: Traditionally considered a Vajikarana (vitality-promoting) herb for men and women.

uses.title: Stress research
uses.detail: Several small clinical trials suggest root extracts may lower perceived stress and cortisol; evidence is still limited.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita - used in Vata disorders and as a Balya herb

preparations.name: Churna (root powder)
preparations.method: Dry roots are powdered finely and taken with warm milk, ghee or honey.

preparations.name: Ashwagandha ghrita / taila
preparations.method: Medicated ghee for internal use or medicated oil for massage, prepared by classical methods.

preparations.name: Ashwagandharishta
preparations.method: A classical fermented tonic prepared from the root with sugar and herbs.
preparations.note: Contains a small natural alcohol content.

preparations.name: Milk decoction (kshirapaka)
preparations.method: Simmer root powder in milk and water until the water evaporates; strain and drink warm.

precautions: Avoid in pregnancy because it has been traditionally and experimentally linked to miscarriage risk. May add to the effects of sedatives, thyroid medicines, blood-sugar and blood-pressure medicines and immunosuppressants. People with thyroid disorders, autoimmune disease or nightshade (Solanaceae) allergy should consult a doctor. Large amounts may upset the stomach, and rare liver injury has been reported with supplements. Considered heating, so use cautiously in excess Pitta conditions.

cultivation.climate: Semi-arid tropical to subtropical; tolerates 20-35 C
cultivation.soil: Sandy loam or light red soil with good drainage, pH 7-8
cultivation.propagation: Seeds, sown at the start of the monsoon
cultivation.harvest: Roots dug after 5-6 months when leaves begin to yellow and berries ripen

conservation_status: Not globally threatened, but wild stock is declining from overcollection; cultivation is encouraged.
fun_fact: The name Ashwagandha literally means 'smell of a horse', and the root's strong odour is said to impart horse-like vigour.

regions.name: Central India (Madhya Pradesh)
regions.note: Major growing region, Mandsaur and Neemuch belt

regions.name: Gujarat
regions.note: Wild and cultivated in dry areas

regions.name: North Africa & Egypt
regions.note: Native in the dry Mediterranean south
